newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Japan's love affair with US not over.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Japan's love affair with US not over.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries will remain the favourite destination for Japanese money, despite a scare sparked by comments from Japan's prime minister, analysts said on Tuesday.
Ryutaro Hashimoto said in New York on Monday he hoped the U.S. would co-operate to maintain exchange stability so that Japan would not be tempted to sell Treasuries and buy gold instead.
Treasuries dropped a quarter point and the Dow Jones Industrial Average suffered its second biggest one-day drop in history after his remarks.
"Treasuries have had their chance to react to Hashimoto's comments so I wouldn't imagine there would be any further follow through," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase in London.
At 1117 GMT, the U.S. long bond was quoted at 99-05 to yield 6.69 percent, up from 99-03 in Tokyo and 98-31 at the close in New York on Monday.
Analysts said Hashimoto's comments were not likely to prompt Japanese government institutions to dump Treasuries.

"Hashimoto seemed to imply that Japanese official sources might sell Treasuries which is highly unlikely," said Rob Hayward, economic adviser at BankAmerica in London. "He seems determined to stabilise the yen and that would have completely the opposite effect as we saw overnight with the yen strengthening."
The dollar/yen was at 114.66/76, having slipped to 114.10 overnight and compared with 115.30/35 in late Europe on Monday.
Hayward said private institutions would also be reluctant to sell their U.S. holdings given that the Japanese Ministry of Finance (MOF) had previously encouraged overseas investment.
Indeed the MOF downplayed Hashimoto's comments, saying Japan had not sold Treasuries and had no intention of doing so.
However if the yen strengthened Japanese investors might be less tempted by Treasuries and might take some profits, Hayward said.
"But that is something which is out of the hands of the government and which has always been there," Hayward said.
Only if there was an escalation in diplomatic tension would this view be changed, analysts said.

"Throughout the day Japanese officials will probably be downplaying the importance of the comments," said Hayward. "The key will be what Rubin says this afternoon and I imagine he will also try to calm the waters."
He said if that was the case the U.S. market was expected to gradually claw back some of its losses.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin will speak to a forum on the American City at 1315 GMT in Washington and was expected to be asked about the overnight developments.

Hashimoto's comments sent the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbling 192.25 points or 2.5 percent to 7604.26. But unless this developed into a longer term rout bonds were not likely to benefit, analysts said.

"The question for equities is whether the mutual fund money continues to pour in or whether it sits on the sidelines for a while," said Ian Harwood, head of strategy and economics at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson Securities in London.
"I doubt whether it will go into Treasuries rather than equities. People think equities can do nothing but go up in a straight line."
He said while the events of the last 24 hours might bring that view into question, investors were likely to stay in cash and equities rather than switching to bonds.
Schmidt said the fact that the stock market reacted more than Treasuries said more about the condition of equities than about Hashimoto's comments.
"I don't think the comments that were made give any reason to suppose that they would trigger flows from equities to Treasuries," he said.
But analysts said investors in Treasuries should not get complacent as the market was nearing the top of its range.

"Even though the inflation numbers have been very good the strength of the economy is likely to continue," said Schmidt. "The weakness of the second quarter is likely to be temporary and a return to above trend growth is probably going to lead to yields rising through to the end of the year."
